extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, students, and copyeditors seeking guidance on English grammar and word usage
extracted.subtask_description: Concise dictionary-style usage entries giving preferred meanings, distinctions between commonly confused words, recommended phrasing, and examples for standard written English. Designed to help authors and editors choose correct words and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: canon
rubrics_metrics.description: A canon is (1) a general rule or principle, (2) an established criterion, (3) the sum of a writer or composer’s work, (4) the collective literature accepted by a scholastic discipline, (5) a piece of music in which a tune is started by one performer and is mimicked by each of the others, or (6) a Christian priest having special duties within a church or cathedral.

rubrics_metrics.name: capital; capitol
rubrics_metrics.description: A capital is a seat of government (usually a city). A capitol is a building in which a legislature meets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jefferson City is the capital of Missouri. The legislature opened its new session in the capitol today.

rubrics_metrics.name: carat; karat; caret
rubrics_metrics.description: Carat measures the weight of a gemstone; karat measures the purity of gold; caret is a mark on a manuscript indicating where matter is to be inserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To remember: think of 24K gold for karat. Caret literally means '(something) is lacking.' In British English, carat serves in both senses of carat/karat.

rubrics_metrics.name: career; careen
rubrics_metrics.description: Career as a verb meaning 'to go full speed' has largely been assumed in American English by careen, while in British English both verbs may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American English: typically careened down the hill; British English: careered down the hill.

rubrics_metrics.name: case
rubrics_metrics.description: Multifaceted word often overused as a near-synonym of situation; has specialized senses in law (lawsuit or judicial opinion), medicine (instance of disease), container, argument, or grammatical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in case = 'if'; in most cases = 'usually'; in every case = 'always'. Use carefully to avoid verbal inflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: cause célèbre
rubrics_metrics.description: Most strictly denotes a legal case, especially a prosecution, that draws great public interest; by extension, a notorious episode, event, or person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retains accents; now considered naturalized enough not to be italicized except when called out as a phrase. Plural: causes célèbres.

rubrics_metrics.name: censer; censor; sensor
rubrics_metrics.description: Censer: container for burning incense or person who carries it. Censor: person who suppresses objectionable subject matter. Sensor: mechanical/electronic device detecting light, heat, movement, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: censor (vb.); censure (vb.)
rubrics_metrics.description: To censor is to review and remove objectionable material; to censure is to criticize strongly or officially reprimand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soldiers' letters are often censored in wartime; the House of Representatives censured the president for the invasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: center around
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrasing 'centeraround' is illogical; prefer center on or revolve around.

rubrics_metrics.name: certainty; certitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty = firm conviction; certitude = assurance of being certain (trait applied to people). A fact you are sure about is a certainty, not a certitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: chair; chairman; chairwoman; chairperson
rubrics_metrics.description: Chair is widely regarded as the best gender-neutral choice; chair has referred to an office of authority since the mid-seventeenth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also other related entries (5.251-60).

rubrics_metrics.name: childish; childlike
rubrics_metrics.description: Childlike is positive (innocence, eagerness, freshness). Childish is pejorative (immaturity, silliness, unreasonableness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a childlike smile; childish ranting.

rubrics_metrics.name: chord; cord
rubrics_metrics.description: Chord: (1) group of harmonically consonant notes, (2) straight line joining ends of an arc (mathematical). Cord: thick string/rope, enclosed wire, or quantity of firewood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: major chords; spinal cord; vocal cord.

rubrics_metrics.name: circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Both 'in the circumstances' and 'under the circumstances' are acceptable; 'under the circumstances' more common in American English; 'in' predominates in British English.

rubrics_metrics.name: cite (n.); site
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun, 'cite' is colloquial for citation (a source). 'Site' is a place or location for a particular purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a cite to Encyclopaedia Britannica; building site; website. Cf. sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: citizen; subject
rubrics_metrics.description: In government sense, citizen owes allegiance to a nation (sovereignty collective), subject owes allegiance to an individual sovereign (monarchical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a citizen of Germany; a subject of the queen.

rubrics_metrics.name: class
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes a category or group of things considered together because of similarities; properly a class is never 'one type' or 'one kind of thing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the class of woodwind instruments; the oboe is a type of woodwind.

rubrics_metrics.name: classic; classical
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic = important, authoritative, outstanding. Classical = relating to traditional values in literature, music, design, or the definitive earliest form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Naked Night is one of Ingmar Bergman's classic films; classical Greek; a classical composer.

rubrics_metrics.name: clean; cleanse
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean has displaced cleanse in many literal senses; cleanse retains sense of 'pure' and usually refers to spiritual/moral purification.

rubrics_metrics.name: cleave
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally two different words with opposite meanings: (1) to cut apart; (2) to cling together; conjugations differ by sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contronym example; conjugations: (1) cleave, cleft (or clove), cleft (or cloven); (2) cleave, cleaved, cleaved.

rubrics_metrics.name: clench; clinch
rubrics_metrics.description: Clench connotes a physical action (hands, teeth, jaw); clinch more common in figurative uses meaning to finally achieve something after a struggle; also can be physical (boxing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: he clenched his hand into a fist; clinched the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: climactic; climatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Climactic = pertaining to climax; climatic = pertaining to climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: movie's climactic scene; the climatic conditions of northern New Mexico.

rubrics_metrics.name: close proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundant phrase; use either close or in proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: closure; cloture
rubrics_metrics.description: Closure = temporary or permanent closing or final resolution; cloture = parliamentary procedure of closing debate and taking a vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: cohabit; cohabitate
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohabit is the traditional verb for living with another in a sexual relationship without marriage; cohabitate is a back-formation and is best avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: collaborate; corroborate
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborate = cooperate on an undertaking; corroborate = back up reliability with proof or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the participants are collaborators; the expert corroborated the witness's testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: collegial; collegiate
rubrics_metrics.description: Collegial relates to colleagues (healthy collegial work environment); collegiate relates to college (collegiate sports).

rubrics_metrics.name: commendable; commendatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Commendable = done for a worthy cause; commendatory = expresses praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commendable dedication; commendatory plaque.

rubrics_metrics.name: common; mutual
rubrics_metrics.description: Common = shared by two or more people; mutual = reciprocal or directly exchanged by and toward each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'friend in common' rather than 'mutual friend' when referring to a third person who is a friend of two others.

rubrics_metrics.name: commonweal; commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonweal = public welfare. Commonwealth traditionally = a state established by public compact to promote commonweal; in U.S. usage synonymous with state for some states and territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Commonwealth of Puerto Rico; four U.S. states called commonwealths.

rubrics_metrics.name: compare with; compare to
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare with = discern both similarities and differences; compare to = liken things or note primarily similarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Are you comparing me to him?

rubrics_metrics.name: compelled; impelled
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelled = no choice (outside force). Impelled = inner drive or conviction (may still dislike it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Nixon was compelled by the unanimous Supreme Court decision to turn over the tapes; the voter was impelled by the income-tax issue to vote a straight-party ticket.

rubrics_metrics.name: compendious; voluminous
rubrics_metrics.description: Compendious = concise, abridged. Voluminous = vast or extremely lengthy (literally occupying many volumes).

rubrics_metrics.name: complacent; complaisant; compliant
rubrics_metrics.description: Complacent = content (possibly smug) and unwilling to improve; complaisant = eager to please others; compliant = amenable to orders or regimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: compliment; complement
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliment = flattering remark; complement = something that completes. As verbs: to compliment = to praise; to complement = to supplement or complete. Adjectives: complimentary vs complementary have different senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a compliment on your skill; the lace tablecloth was a complement to the antique silver. Complimentary = expressing praise or free; complementary = going well together or geometric angles summing to 90 degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: comprise; compose
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprise = to consist of, to include (the whole comprises the parts). Compose = to make up; the parts compose the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'is comprised of' (nonstandard); prefer 'is composed of' or 'consists of.'

rubrics_metrics.name: concept; conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Both may refer to an abstract thought; conception also means the act of forming an abstract thought. Avoid as high-sounding equivalents of idea, design, thought, or program.

rubrics_metrics.name: condole; console
rubrics_metrics.description: Condole = express sympathy (with); console = comfort in distress or disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nouns: condolence (they expressed their condolences); consolation (their kind words were small consolation). Example: community leaders condoled with the victims' families.

rubrics_metrics.name: confidant; confidante; confident
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidant = close companion you confide in; confidante = feminine form (fading). Confident = adjective meaning 'sure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: congruous; congruent
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruous = in harmony or agreement (often seen as incongruous). Congruent = used in math to describe identical angles/side lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: incongruous modern house in old neighborhood; congruent angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: connote; denote
rubrics_metrics.description: Connote = convey meaning beyond the basic one, often emotive. Denote = specify the literal meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: parenting and all that it connotes; the phrase freezing point denotes 32°F.

rubrics_metrics.name: consequent; subsequent
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequent denotes causation (happens as result). Subsequent denotes only temporal order (may be unrelated).

rubrics_metrics.name: consider (use of 'as')
rubrics_metrics.description: Add 'as' only when you mean 'to examine or discuss for a particular purpose'; otherwise omit 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: handshaking considered as a means of spreading disease vs we consider him qualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: consist of; consist in
rubrics_metrics.description: Consist of = physical components making up a tangible thing. Consist in = essence of a thing, especially abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the computer-system package consists of software, CPU, monitor, and printer; moral government consists in rewarding the righteous.

rubrics_metrics.name: contact (vb.)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you mean write or call or email, say so; 'contact' is a brief way to refer to communication without specifying means.

rubrics_metrics.name: contagious; infectious
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagious = spreads by direct contact with infected person/animal. Infectious = spread by germs on contaminated objects or elements (may be noncontagious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rabies is contagious; tetanus is infectious but not contagious.

rubrics_metrics.name: contemporary; contemporaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary usually applies to people and also can mean modern; contemporaneous applies to things or actions coinciding in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous uses: replace 'contemporary' with 'modern' when multiple times are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: contemptuous; contemptible
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemptuous = feeling/showing disdain (someone you scorn). Contemptible = deserving contempt (others will look down on you).

rubrics_metrics.name: content; contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Content = ideas, facts, opinions in a presentation. Contents = physical things inside a container or list of items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the lecture's content; table of contents; the package's contents were difficult to discern by x-ray.

rubrics_metrics.name: continual; continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual = repeated with brief interruptions (intermittent). Continuous = uninterrupted, never stops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: continual nagging vs continuous flow of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: contravene; controvert
rubrics_metrics.description: Contravene = conflict with or violate (law/rule). Controvert = challenge or contradict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: higher speed limit contravenes our policy; the testimony controverts prior statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: copyright (vb.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verb meaning to obtain legal right to be the only producer or seller of a creative work for a specific time; conjugated copyright-copyrighted-copyrighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spelling has nothing to do with 'write'.

rubrics_metrics.name: corollary; correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary = subsidiary proposition following from a proven proposition or a natural result. Correlation = positive connection between things; degree to which interactions not attributable to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In physics/statistics, correlation denotes observed interactions/variances beyond chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: corporal; corporeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporal relates in some way to the body (e.g., corporal punishment). Corporeal means having a physical form that can be touched.

rubrics_metrics.name: corps; core
rubrics_metrics.description: Corps = body of like workers (often misspelled like 'core'). Core = central or most important part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Marine Corps; press corps; the core of the problem; the earth's core.

rubrics_metrics.name: couldn't care less
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard phrasing; avoid the illogical form 'could care less'.

rubrics_metrics.name: councillor; counselor
rubrics_metrics.description: Councillor = one who sits on a council. Counselor = one whose job is to help and advise people; British spelling counsellor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: city councillor; personal counselor.

rubrics_metrics.name: couple
rubrics_metrics.description: Using couple as adjective traditionally nonstandard though increasingly common; when referring to two people as a unit the noun may take singular or plural verb depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add 'of' in some casual uses: a couple of movies. Examples: the couple is happy; the couple are honeymooning. When pronoun they follows, plural verb preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words joined by a hyphen as noun or verb; plural of noun is courts-martial; third-person-singular verb is court-martials; inflected verb forms differ American vs British spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American verb forms: court-martialed, court-martialing; British: court-martialled, court-martialling.

rubrics_metrics.name: credible; creditable; credulous
rubrics_metrics.description: Credible = believable/deserving trust. Creditable = praiseworthy/deserving approval. Credulous = gullible, easily deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cliché note: avoid 'strains credulity'; prefer 'strains credibility.'

rubrics_metrics.name: crevice; crevasse
rubrics_metrics.description: Crevice = narrow, not very deep crack (sidewalk). Crevasse = deep open crack (glacier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation and size distinction: crevice (accent first syllable); crevasse (accent second syllable).

rubrics_metrics.name: criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural form of criterion (= a standard for judging). One criterion, two criteria. 'Criterias' is wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: damp (vb.); dampen
rubrics_metrics.description: Both convey 'to moisten.' Damp also means 'to reduce with moisture' or 'to diminish vibration/oscillation'; dampen figuratively means to make less intense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: damp the fire; damp the voltage; dampen one's hopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: data
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally plural of datum; now commonly treated as a mass noun with singular verb. In formal writing and always in the sciences, use data as a plural. Use consistently within a single writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: deadly; deathly
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadly = capable of causing death or likely to cause great harm. Deathly = arousing thoughts of death or a dead body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deadly snake venom; deathly silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: decimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Literally meant 'to kill every tenth person' historically; now often means to inflict heavy damage. Avoid using to mean complete destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say a city was completely decimated when you mean destroyed entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: defamation; libel; slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation = communication of a falsehood that damages reputation. If recorded, especially in writing, it's libel; otherwise slander.

rubrics_metrics.name: definite; definitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Definite = clear, exact. Definitive = not subject to further revision soon or of such high quality as to be unimprovable for a long time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a definite yes; a definitive guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: deliberate (adj.); deliberative
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate = planned/carefully thought out or slow and steady. Deliberative = involving debate, applies to assemblies or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a deliberate response; deliberative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: denounce; renounce
rubrics_metrics.description: Denounce = criticize harshly or accuse (inform to authorities). Renounce = relinquish or publicly declare rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: they denounced the prisoner swap; renounced her citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: dependant (n.); dependent (adj. & n.)
rubrics_metrics.description: In British English 'dependant' is the preferable noun; 'dependent' is the adjective. In American English 'dependent' is usual as both noun and adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: he claimed three dependants on his tax return (British).

rubrics_metrics.name: depend on
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'on' rather than 'upon' in this phrase; 'depend' demands an 'on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: That depends on how we approach the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: deprecate
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally to strongly disapprove or criticize. In 'self-deprecating' the sense is 'to belittle.' In computing 'deprecate' warns that a feature may be phased out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In computing, deprecated features signal users should look for alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: derisive; derisory
rubrics_metrics.description: Derisive = ridicules as stupid or silly. Derisory = invites or deserves ridicule, often meaning laughably small amount (esp. money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: derisive laughter; derisory paychecks.

rubrics_metrics.name: deserts; desserts
rubrics_metrics.description: Deserts = what is deserved. Desserts = sweet course eaten. 'Just desserts' often misspelled (unless meaning postprandial sweets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: he got his just deserts.

rubrics_metrics.name: despite; in spite of
rubrics_metrics.description: For brevity, prefer despite.

rubrics_metrics.name: determine whether; determine if
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Determine whether' is irreproachable style; 'determine if' acceptable as colloquialism. Same for 'decide whether' vs 'decide if.'

rubrics_metrics.name: different
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Different from' is generally preferable to 'different than'; British English uses 'different to' sometimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'differently than' when adverbial sense is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: differ from; differ with
rubrics_metrics.description: Differ from = denote a contrast. Differ with = differences of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the two species differ from each other; the state's senators differ with each other on many issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: disburse; disperse
rubrics_metrics.description: Disburse = distribute money. Disperse = spread widely or cause to go away in different directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disburse funds; the clouds dispersed; police dispersed the unruly crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: discomfort; discomfit
rubrics_metrics.description: Discomfort = noun meaning 'ill at ease' or verb 'to put ill at ease.' Discomfit originally meant 'to defeat utterly' and now means 'to thwart, confuse, annoy, or embarrass.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'discomfort' as a verb may invite confusion with 'discomfit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: discreet; discrete
rubrics_metrics.description: Discreet = careful about not divulging secrets or tasteful/modest. Discrete = separate, distinct, unconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: six discrete parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: discriminating; discriminatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Discriminatory = reflecting biased, unfair treatment. Discriminating = analytically refined, discerning, tasteful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: discriminatory employment policy vs a discriminating palate.

rubrics_metrics.name: disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: Should be reserved for 'not having a personal financial interest and therefore impartial.' Avoid using it to mean 'uninterested.'

rubrics_metrics.name: disk; disc
rubrics_metrics.description: Disk is usual spelling (hard disk). Disc preferred in some specialized applications (compact disc, disc brakes), especially when object is circular and flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: disorganized; unorganized
rubrics_metrics.description: Both mean 'not organized,' but disorganized suggests disarray or inherent inability to work together or a person bad at arranging; unorganized lacks that nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the disorganized 1968 Democratic National Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: distinctive; distinguished; distinguishable
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctive = makes person/place easy to recognize. Distinguished = respected and admired. Distinguishable = easy to see as different; lacks positive connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: U2's distinctive sound; the distinguished professor; the person distinguishable from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: dive (verb forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred conjugation historically dive-dived-dived; irregular form dove has become slightly predominant past tense in American English and is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionalists may stick to dive-dived-dived; dive-dove-dived is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: doctrinal; doctrinaire
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal = relating to or constituting a doctrine (neutral). Doctrinaire = dogmatic, stubborn, narrow-minded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: doctrinaire ideologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: doubtfully (adv.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Used in recent years as a sentence adverb correlating to hopefully and as antonym of undoubtedly (e.g., 'Hopefully—but doubtfully').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard advice: Should you abstain from this usage in Standard Written English? No doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: doubtless (adv.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'doubtless' (flat adverb), not 'doubtlessly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 5.160 (not included here).

rubrics_metrics.name: doubt that; doubt whether; doubt if
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Doubt that' conveys strong skepticism. 'Doubt whether' conveys skepticism but less strong. 'Doubt if' is casual for 'doubt that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: I doubt that you'll ever get your money back; he doubts whether the company could survive.

rubrics_metrics.name: drag (verb forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugated drag-dragged-dragged. Past form 'drug' is dialectal.

rubrics_metrics.name: dream (verb forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either dreamed (more typical) or dreamt is acceptable for past-tense and past-participial forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: drink (verb forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctly conjugated drink-drank-drunk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: they had not drunk any fruit juice that day.

rubrics_metrics.name: drown (verb forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugated drown-drowned-drowned.

rubrics_metrics.name: drunk (adj.); drunken
rubrics_metrics.description: Drunk describes a current state of intoxication (a drunk driver). Drunken describes habitual intoxication or intoxicated people's behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a drunk; drunken sot; a drunken brawl.

rubrics_metrics.name: dual; duel
rubrics_metrics.description: Dual = having two parts or two of something. Duel = a fight between two people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dual exhaust vs a duel.

rubrics_metrics.name: due to
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally interchangeable with attributable to or owed to when interchangeable with adjective 'attributable'; adverbial uses often inferior to because of or owing to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Due to the parents' negligence → Better: Because of the parents' negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: due to the fact that
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbose phrasing; use 'because' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: dumb
rubrics_metrics.description: Means either 'stupid' or 'unable to speak'; use 'mute' when meaning 'unable to speak' to avoid offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: on noun use of 'mute', see 'moot' entry (not included here).

rubrics_metrics.name: dying; dyeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Dying = present participle of die. Dyeing = present participle of dye (to color with a liquid).

rubrics_metrics.name: each (subject-verb agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun serving as the subject of a clause, 'each' takes a singular verb. When it serves as an emphatic appositive for a plural noun, the verb is plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Each of them was present. They each have their virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: each other; one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionalists: each other for two, one another for more than two.

rubrics_metrics.name: eatable
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'edible' (i.e., prefer edible).

rubrics_metrics.name: economic; economical
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic = relating to large-scale finances. Economical = thrifty, financially efficient, not wasteful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: federal economic policy; an economical purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: edible; eatable
rubrics_metrics.description: Edible = fit for human consumption. Eatable = at least minimally palatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: edible flowers; the cake is slightly burned but still eatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: effete
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally 'worn out, sterile' or 'lacking power'; now often used to mean 'snobbish' or 'effeminate'; ambiguous so best avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: effrontery; affront
rubrics_metrics.description: Effrontery = shameless impudence or shocking audacity. Affront = deliberate insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: e.g.
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviated form of et alii? (Note: actually et alii = 'and others'; e.g. = exempli gratia 'for example'). (Entry cross-ref says see i.e.)

rubrics_metrics.name: either (agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like neither, this word takes a singular verb when it functions as subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Is either of the spouses present today?

rubrics_metrics.name: elemental; elementary
rubrics_metrics.description: Elemental = essential constituent or power of nature. Elementary = basic, introductory, or easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an elementary math problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: elicit; illicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Elicit = to draw out or get (information/reaction); illicit = disallowed by law or socially condemned. Writers often mistakenly use illicit when they need elicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to elicit responses; an illicit scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: embarrass
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'harass' (cross-ref).

rubrics_metrics.name: emend
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'amend' (cross-ref).

rubrics_metrics.name: emigrate
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'immigrate' (cross-ref).

rubrics_metrics.name: eminent; imminent
rubrics_metrics.description: Eminent = famous, important, respected. Imminent = looming and likely to happen soon, almost always bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the eminent professor; imminent disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: emoji; emoticon
rubrics_metrics.description: Emoji = pictorial ideogram (face, hand gesture, object) expressing emotion or ideas. Emoticon = representation of a smiley face rendered by keyboard characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example emoticon: ;-)

rubrics_metrics.name: emotive; emotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotive = arousing intense feeling (often used to persuade). Emotional = relating to or involving intense feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: emotive language calculated to persuade the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: empathy; sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Empathy = ability to understand others' feelings. Sympathy = compassion/sorrow for another's misfortune or support for an idea; can also mean mutual understanding/arising from compatibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tremendous empathy with others; our sympathies are with you.

rubrics_metrics.name: endemic; epidemic; pandemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epidemic = outbreak in limited area that spreads then subsides. Endemic = perennially present within a region/population (describes disease, not region). Pandemic = prevalent over large area or world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: measles epidemic; malaria is endemic in parts of Africa; 1918-19 flu pandemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: endorse
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'approve' (cross-ref).

rubrics_metrics.name: enervate; innervate
rubrics_metrics.description: Enervate = to weaken or drain of energy. Innervate = to stimulate or provide with energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: enormity; enormousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Enormity = monstrousness, moral outrageousness. Enormousness = hugeness or immensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: enormity of the Khmer Rouge's killings vs the enormousness of Alaska.

rubrics_metrics.name: ensure; insure; assure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure = make sure something will happen. Insure = underwrite financial risk. Assure = tell people something to relieve worry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure events and insure things; assure people.

rubrics_metrics.name: enthused
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'enthusiastic' instead of 'enthused.'

rubrics_metrics.name: enumerable; innumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerable = countable/listable. Innumerable = cannot be counted practically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because pronunciation is similar, be wary in speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: envy
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'jealousy' (cross-ref).

rubrics_metrics.name: equally as
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically faulty phrasing; delete 'as' (use 'equally').

rubrics_metrics.name: et al.
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation of et alii ('and others') — the 'others' are people, not things. 'al.' is an abbreviation and requires a period; no period follows 'et'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cf. etc.; note that et al. should not be used for things.

rubrics_metrics.name: etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation of et cetera ('and other things'); never use in reference to people. Often misused as a filler when writers run out of thoughts. Avoid redundancy with 'and etc.' or using after 'for example, such as, e.g.,' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: do not write 'and etc.'; 'etc.' implies a list of things is too extensive to recite.

rubrics_metrics.name: event
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase 'in the event that' is verbose and formal; prefer 'if.'

rubrics_metrics.name: eventuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Often needlessly displaces more specific words such as event, result, possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more specific everyday words.

rubrics_metrics.name: every day; everyday
rubrics_metrics.description: Every day (adverbial) vs everyday (adjectival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may wear your everyday clothes every day.

rubrics_metrics.name: every one; everyone
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-word 'every one' is emphatic meaning 'each of'; 'everyone' is pronoun equivalent to 'everybody'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: every one of them was there; everyone was there.

rubrics_metrics.name: everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'everywhere' over 'everyplace.'

rubrics_metrics.name: evoke; invoke
rubrics_metrics.description: Evoke = bring out or bring to mind. Invoke = assert as authority, appeal for help, or conjure up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: evoke laughter; invoke the Monroe Doctrine; invoke spirits of the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: exceptional; exceptionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional = uncommon, superior, rare. Exceptionable = objectionable or offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an exceptional talent vs an exceptionable slur.

rubrics_metrics.name: executor; administrator
rubrics_metrics.description: In a will a person designates an executor to distribute the estate. When dying without a will or designated executor, the court appoints an administrator. Feminine forms executrix/administratrix unnecessary.
